When Every Job Lands on the Same Few People, Software Has to Pull More Weight

Last updated: September 18, 2026
Renee Johnson
Image Credit: Magnific
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:24
Instaread

Small organizations can accumulate software surprisingly fast. Someone adds a payment tool because money needs to come in more smoothly. Another system appears later because communication is getting messy. Before long, the team has plenty of technology and is still copying information by hand.

The problem becomes more obvious when there are only a few people around to absorb the extra work. Every login and repeated task takes time away from the work customers or communities actually see.

Churches deal with this constantly. Many operate with lean staffs while managing donations and large groups of people whose information changes throughout the year. Tithely has built its business around reducing some of that administrative load, growing from a mobile giving app into a complete church management platform now used by more than 53,000 churches worldwide.

The industry may be specialized, but the operating problem should sound familiar to anyone running a small business alone or with a handful of employees. Software is supposed to save labor. Once managing the software becomes another job, something has gone wrong.

Tool Hopping Has a Labor Cost

The cost of using several systems is easy to underestimate because each task looks small on its own.

Moving a name from one database into another may take less than a minute. Checking whether an event registration matches a payment takes a little longer. Multiply those moments across a week and the organization starts paying for software twice: once with money and again with staff attention.

Tithely has moved toward combining more of that work inside one platform. Its All Access product puts giving alongside church management, while communication tools live in the same system. Churches can also handle volunteer scheduling and children’s check-in without building separate processes around each one.

For a lean team, the appeal is the reduction in handoffs. When information already lives where the next task happens, somebody does not have to move it there first.

That is a useful standard for self-employed people evaluating their own software. Feature count tells you very little about how much time a product will save. The better question is how often the tool removes a step you currently perform yourself.

A scheduling app that still requires you to copy customer information into another system has only solved part of the problem. The same goes for payment software that creates another record you later have to reconcile.

Good software should slowly make those invisible jobs disappear.

Integration Matters More When There Is Nobody to Delegate To

Large companies can sometimes hide inefficient software behind headcount. If two systems do not talk to each other, somebody can be assigned to bridge them.

A solo operator does not have that luxury, and neither does a church staff where the same person may be handling administration in the morning and helping with an event later that day.

Tithely’s growth reflects that reality. The company began with one narrow giving problem after co-founder Dean Sweetman saw how easily a mobile phone could handle an everyday purchase and wondered why church donations still involved so much friction. His son built the first version in six months, and the product eventually expanded as the company encountered more of the work sitting around that original transaction.

Today, Tithely sells a bundled platform that connects giving with administrative tools rather than asking churches to assemble every part separately. Its current All Access plan is explicitly built around reducing “tool-hopping,” which is a revealing way to describe the problem.

Small-business owners often shop for software one frustration at a time, so the same kind of sprawl can build almost accidentally. One subscription fixes invoicing. Six months later, another fixes scheduling. Each purchase is reasonable until the owner realizes they spend part of every Friday making the systems agree with each other.

There is no prize for running the largest software stack.

The better setup is usually the one that leaves fewer loose ends for a person to pick up. For a self-employed worker, that can mean choosing a product that handles two closely connected jobs well instead of buying separate tools that create another transfer of information.

Tithely operates in church technology, yet the lesson travels easily. Lean organizations get more value from software when it reduces coordination instead of creating more of it. The people doing the work already have enough jobs.
